## Overview

The earlier pages describe the market, compare it with our team's skills, and model pay. This page turns
those results into a **plan for a student or early-career job seeker** on the **Data Analyst to Data
Scientist** pathway in NAICS 5182 (Computing Infrastructure Providers, Data Processing, Web Hosting, and
Related Services). It answers the last research question of the project: **what should a job seeker learn
first, and where should they apply?**

Everything here comes from the 765 pathway postings in the MET Career Compass 2026 jobs data (see
[Data Preparation](data_preparation.qmd)), from the models on the [Predictive
Modeling](predictive_modeling.qmd) page, and from the team skill comparison on the [Skill Gap
Analysis](skill_gap_analysis.qmd) page. It also feeds the written final report. The patterns are
associations in posted jobs, not promises about any one offer; the last section lists the limits.

**The short version:**

1. Enter through the analyst toolkit (SQL, visualization, communication) and show it in a portfolio.
2. Make Machine Learning and Python the bridge to Data Scientist and ML Engineer roles. This is where the
   largest pay difference is.
3. Add cloud and data-pipeline skills, which this industry values, and document your experience early.

```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go

PALETTE = ["#457b9d", "#2a9d8f", "#e9c46a", "#e76f51", "#6d597a", "#f4a261"]
GRAY = "#b8bec6"


def style(fig, title, subtitle, height=450, legend=False):
    fig.update_layout(
        title=dict(text=f"<b>{title}</b><br><span style='font-size:12px;color:gray'>{subtitle}</span>",
                   x=0, xanchor="left"),
        template="simple_white", height=height, showlegend=legend,
        font=dict(family="Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif", size=13),
        margin=dict(l=10, r=20, t=95, b=50), hoverlabel=dict(bgcolor="white", font_size=13),
        legend=dict(orientation="h", x=0.5, xanchor="center", y=-0.15, yanchor="top"))
    fig.update_xaxes(gridcolor="#eceff3")
    fig.update_yaxes(gridcolor="#eceff3")
    return fig


def show(fig):
    fig.show(config={"displaylogo": False, "responsive": True, "modeBarButtonsToRemove": ["lasso2d", "select2d"]})


mp = pd.read_csv("data/processed/met_text_panel.csv")
mp["salary_mid"] = (mp["salary_min_annual"] + mp["salary_max_annual"]) / 2
SENIOR = r"senior|\bsr\b|staff|principal|\blead\b|manager|director|head of|architect"
mp["level"] = np.where(mp["title"].str.lower().str.contains(SENIOR), "Senior title", "Other title")
tx = mp[mp["has_text"]].copy()
skill_cols = [c for c in mp.columns if c.startswith("skill_")]

# the same team ratings used on the Skill Gap Analysis page
team = pd.DataFrame({
    "Python": [5, 3, 4], "SQL": [5, 4, 3], "Machine Learning": [3, 3, 5],
    "Cloud/AWS": [4, 5, 3], "Data Visualization": [4, 3, 5], "Statistics": [2, 4, 3],
}, index=["Manan Patel", "Richard Park", "Michael Phillips"])
team_avg = team.mean()
roles = ["Data Analyst", "Data / Analytics Engineer", "Data Scientist", "ML Engineer"]
```

## The Four Roles at a Glance

The pathway has four role families. The table puts the main facts for each in one place, using the same
scoring as the [Role Opportunity Scorecard](predictive_modeling.qmd) (pay 40%, accessibility 30%, fit with
our team 30%).

```{python}
#| label: roles-at-a-glance
rows = []
for role in roles:
    g, t = mp[mp["role"] == role], tx[tx["role"] == role]
    demand = {s: t["skill_" + s].astype(bool).mean() for s in team_avg.index}
    top = (t[skill_cols].astype(bool).mean().sort_values(ascending=False).head(3))
    no_grad = 1 - (t["degree_Master"].isin(["required", "preferred"]) | t["degree_PhD"].isin(["required", "preferred"])).mean()
    rows.append({
        "Role": role, "Postings": len(g), "With salary": int(g["salary_mid"].notna().sum()),
        "Median posted pay": g["salary_mid"].median(),
        "Typical experience asked (years)": g["experience_min_years"].median(),
        "Not a senior title": (g["level"] == "Other title").mean(),
        "Most-named skills": ", ".join(s[len("skill_"):] for s in top.index),
        "pay": g["salary_mid"].median(),
        "access": ((g["level"] == "Other title").mean() + no_grad) / 2,
        "fit": sum(demand[s] * team_avg[s] for s in demand) / sum(demand.values()) / 5,
    })
glance = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Role")
glance["Opportunity score"] = 0.4 * glance["pay"] / glance["pay"].max() + 0.3 * glance["access"] + 0.3 * glance["fit"]
glance = glance.sort_values("Opportunity score", ascending=False)
out = glance[["Postings", "With salary", "Median posted pay", "Typical experience asked (years)",
              "Not a senior title", "Most-named skills", "Opportunity score"]].copy()
out["Median posted pay"] = out["Median posted pay"].map("${:,.0f}".format)
out["Typical experience asked (years)"] = out["Typical experience asked (years)"].map("{:.0f}".format)
out["Not a senior title"] = out["Not a senior title"].map("{:.0%}".format)
out["Opportunity score"] = out["Opportunity score"].map("{:.3f}".format)
out
```

**How to read it:** ML Engineer and Data Scientist score highest because they pay the most (median posted pay
of $220,260 and $204,875). Data Analyst is the lowest-paying role (median $114,750) but the most accessible,
since 65% of its postings do not use a senior title. That is the trade-off behind the plan below: start where
the entry is realistic, then move toward the roles that pay more. Pay medians for Data Analyst rest on only 30
postings with a salary, so treat them as a guide.

## A Three-Step Plan

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
### Step 1: Enter through the analyst toolkit

Data Analyst postings most often name communication (35%), SQL (31%), data visualization (21%), Excel (18%),
and dashboards (16%). **Build one portfolio project** that answers a business question with SQL and presents
it in a dashboard with a short written summary. Showing that you can communicate results is part of the
skill, not an extra.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
### Step 2: Use Machine Learning and Python as the bridge

Data Scientist and ML Engineer postings name Machine Learning in 68% of cases and Python in 54%, compared with
11% and 20% for Data Analyst postings. Once the role is known, naming Machine Learning adds comparatively little on its own;
the bigger gain comes from moving into a role that expects it. Moving from a Data Analyst
title to a Data Scientist or ML Engineer title is associated with **roughly $72,000 to $82,000** more in
disclosed pay, which is larger than any location choice. **Complete a supervised-learning project in Python**
that explains how it was evaluated and what its limits are.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
### Step 3: Add cloud and pipeline skills, and document your experience

Cloud/AWS appears in 28% of Data Scientist and ML postings and 55% of Data / Analytics Engineer postings, and
ETL in 68% of engineer postings. A cloud certification and one analysis run on a cloud platform signal fit
with employers in this industry, and Data / Analytics Engineer roles (median posted pay $175,000) are a
second route up the pathway. Because the market skews mid-career, **document internships, research, and
projects in a portfolio** early.
:::

## Which Skills Should You Learn First?

The chart compares how often each skill appears in **Data Analyst** postings with how often it appears in the
postings for the role you want. Use the dropdown to choose a **target role**. The skills are sorted by the
**gap**: the skills at the top are the ones the target role asks for much more often than analyst roles do,
so they are the ones to learn first.

```{python}
#| label: skill-gap-dropdown
analyst = tx[tx["role"] == "Data Analyst"]
a_share = analyst[skill_cols].astype(bool).mean()
targets = ["Data Scientist", "ML Engineer", "Data / Analytics Engineer"]
TOP = 8


def view(role):
    t = tx[tx["role"] == role]
    t_share = t[skill_cols].astype(bool).mean()
    gap = (t_share - a_share).sort_values(ascending=False).head(TOP)
    gap = gap[gap > 0.02][::-1]  # only skills the target role names clearly more often
    names = [c[len("skill_"):] for c in gap.index]
    return dict(names=names, analyst=a_share[gap.index].values, target=t_share[gap.index].values,
                gap=gap.values, n=len(t))


views = {r: view(r) for r in targets}
v0 = views[targets[0]]


def title_for(role):
    return (f"<b>Skills to Learn First: Data Analyst to {role}</b><br><span style='font-size:12px;color:gray'>"
            f"Share of postings naming each skill | up to {TOP} skills with the biggest gap | postings with text "
            f"(Data Analyst n={len(analyst)}, {role} n={views[role]['n']})</span>")


def traces_for(role):
    v = views[role]
    return dict(
        x=[v["analyst"], v["target"]], y=[v["names"], v["names"]],
        text=[[f"{s:.0%}" for s in v["analyst"]], [f"{s:.0%}" for s in v["target"]]],
        customdata=[np.round(v["gap"] * 100), np.round(v["gap"] * 100)])


init = traces_for(targets[0])
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(name="Data Analyst postings", orientation="h", marker_color=GRAY,
                     x=init["x"][0], y=init["y"][0], text=init["text"][0], textposition="outside",
                     customdata=init["customdata"][0],
                     hovertemplate="<b>%{y}</b><br>Data Analyst postings: %{x:.0%}<br>Gap to target: +%{customdata:.0f} points<extra></extra>"))
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(name="Target role postings", orientation="h", marker_color=PALETTE[1],
                     x=init["x"][1], y=init["y"][1], text=init["text"][1], textposition="outside",
                     customdata=init["customdata"][1],
                     hovertemplate="<b>%{y}</b><br>Target role postings: %{x:.0%}<br>Gap to analyst postings: +%{customdata:.0f} points<extra></extra>"))
fig.update_layout(barmode="group", updatemenus=[dict(
    type="dropdown", direction="down", x=0, xanchor="left", y=1.0, yanchor="bottom", showactive=True,
    buttons=[dict(label=f"Target role: {r}", method="update",
                  args=[{k: traces_for(r)[k] for k in ("x", "y", "text", "customdata")},
                        {"title.text": title_for(r)}]) for r in targets])])
fig.update_xaxes(title="Share of postings that name the skill", tickformat=".0%", range=[0, 1])
style(fig, f"Skills to Learn First: Data Analyst to {targets[0]}", "", height=620, legend=True)
fig.update_layout(title_text=title_for(targets[0]), margin=dict(l=10, r=20, t=175, b=60))
show(fig)
```

**Interpretation:** the skills that open the way to a Data Scientist or ML Engineer role are Machine Learning,
Python, and deep learning, while the Data / Analytics Engineer role leans on cloud, ETL, and data modeling
skills. The 68% and 54% quoted in Step 2 pool Data Scientist and ML Engineer postings, while this chart
shows each role separately. Skill shares come from searching the posting text, so they undercount real demand and should be
compared between roles, not read as exact requirements. Compared with our own team (see [Skill Gap
Analysis](skill_gap_analysis.qmd)), the clearest group gaps are **Machine Learning** and **Statistics**, which
is why those come first in our own improvement plan.

## Where to Apply

Demand for this pathway is concentrated. Of the 653 postings with a state we could identify, **California (141)
and New York (113)** together hold about 39%. They also show the highest posted pay among the states with enough postings to compare.

```{python}
#| label: where-to-apply
resolved = mp["state"].notna().sum()
places = ["California", "New York", "Texas", "Virginia", "Washington", "District of Columbia", "Maryland"]
rows = []
for s in places:
    g = mp[mp["state"] == s]
    rows.append({"State": s, "Postings": len(g), "Share of postings with a state": len(g) / resolved,
                 "Postings with salary": int(g["salary_mid"].notna().sum()),
                 "Median posted pay": g["salary_mid"].median()})
where = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("State")
where["Share of postings with a state"] = where["Share of postings with a state"].map("{:.0%}".format)
where["Median posted pay"] = where["Median posted pay"].map(lambda v: f"${v:,.0f}")
where
```

**Interpretation:** California and New York lead on both openings and posted pay (median $224,500 and
$190,000). Virginia, the District of Columbia, and Maryland also have many postings, largely from federal
contractors, at lower posted pay in Virginia and Maryland. The Texas pay figure rests on only 4 postings with a
salary and should not be relied on. Salary-disclosure laws in California and New York also push employers
there to post pay, so those states may look more generous than states where pay is rarely posted. Only about
10% of postings (78 of 765) say the job is remote, and 77% do not state a work arrangement, so **confirm remote
or hybrid policy with the employer** before assuming it.

## What to Expect on Experience and Education

```{python}
#| label: expect
exp = mp["experience_min_years"].dropna()
masters = int((tx["degree_Master"] == "required").sum())
phd = int((tx["degree_PhD"] == "required").sum())
none_named = (tx[[c for c in tx.columns if c.startswith("degree_")]].eq("none").all(axis=1)).mean()
summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "What the postings show": [
        f"{len(exp)} of {len(mp)} postings state an experience requirement; the median is {exp.median():.0f} years",
        f"{((exp >= 3) & (exp <= 8)).mean():.0%} of those ask for 3 to 8 years; {(exp <= 2).mean():.0%} ask for 2 years or fewer",
        f"Of {len(tx)} postings with text, {none_named:.0%} name no degree at all",
        f"A Master's is required in {masters} postings and a PhD in {phd}"],
    "What it means for you": [
        "This is a mid-career market. Few postings describe a new graduate.",
        "Build 1 to 3 years of documented project, internship, or research work before applying to most roles.",
        "A graduate degree is rarely a hard requirement; skills and project evidence matter more.",
        "Apply even if you do not hold the listed graduate degree, if you meet the skills."]})
summary.style.hide(axis="index")
```

Each additional year of experience a posting asks for is associated with about $5,500 more in pay in the
salary estimator, so documented experience matters twice: it opens the door and it moves the estimate up.

## Use the Estimator With This Plan

The [Predictive Modeling](predictive_modeling.qmd) page includes a **salary estimator**. Use it to test the
plan: start with an entry-level analyst profile, then change one thing at a time (the role, the state, a
skill such as Machine Learning, or a senior title) and read which changes are associated with higher pay.
It is a guide to relative differences, not a prediction of what an employer will offer.

## What This Plan Does Not Tell You

- **Associations, not causes.** The pay differences describe patterns in posted jobs. They do not show that
  learning a skill or moving to a state will produce that raise.
- **Small samples.** Only 303 postings state a salary, and 30 of them are Data Analyst postings, so close
  comparisons between roles cannot be separated reliably.
- **Posted pay is not accepted pay.** Disclosure is concentrated in California and New York, which makes
  posted pay look higher than the national median.
- **Text matching.** Skills and degrees are matched from posting text, so the shares are lower bounds.
- **Our own judgment.** The scorecard weights and the Advanced skill target are team choices, and the team
  skill ratings are self-reported by three people.
- **One period.** The data cover January to September 2026, so the plan cannot show trends over time.

See the [Limitations](predictive_modeling.qmd#limitations) on the Predictive Modeling page for the full list.
